system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-01-16 03:45:00 to 2170-01-19 15:14:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted due to inability to tolerate oral intake and significant weight loss from chronic gastrojejunal ulcers following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She underwent placement of a tunneled central line for initiation of total parenteral nutrition. IV pantoprazole was continued to promote ulcer healing, and her nutrition regimen was gradually advanced. Pre-albumin improved slightly, indicating early nutritional recovery. A Chronic Pain consult led to optimization of her pain regimen with increased oxycodone frequency and discontinuation of Roxicet. She tolerated a stage 5 diet by discharge, was stable vitally, and was discharged home on nocturnal TPN with home nursing support and follow-up plans.
problems: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

Constitutional: NAD
Neuro: A&O x 3
Cardiac: RRR, NL S1,S2, No MRG
Lungs: CTA B
Abdomen: soft, non-distended, appropriate ___ 
tenderness, no rebound tenderness or guarding. G-tube in place. 
Right IJ ___ removed, with dressing c/d/i
Ext: No edema

 
Pertinent Results:
___ 04:45AM BLOOD Glucose-154* UreaN-12 Creat-0.7 Na-139 
K-3.9 Cl-104 HCO3-28 AnGap-11 ___ 04:45AM BLOOD Calcium-8.8 
Phos-4.4 Mg-2.2

___ 07:36PM BLOOD Glucose-105* UreaN-12 Creat-0.8 Na-139 
K-3.9 Cl-105 HCO3-26 AnGap-12 ___ 07:36PM BLOOD Calcium-8.8 
Phos-3.8 Mg-2.2
 
Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ ___ s/p gastric bypass ___ with subsequent 
development of gastrojejunal anastomatoic ulcers on TPN via R. 
___, was brought to the OR on ___ for laparoscopic 
gastrostomy (g-tube placement). She had no intraoperative 
complications, and on POD1 her TPN was discontinued. On HD1 a 
post operative gastrograffin study confirmed placement of the 
G-tube, and she was started on tube feeds (fibersource HN) in 
consultation with the nutrition service. She tolerated tube 
feeds well, and her baseline nausea did not worsen while on the 
feeds. On HD3 she was at her goal TF level (80 cc/hr for a 12 
hour cycle at night). ___ was arranged to assist her with home 
tube feeds. On HD3 her R. IJ Hickman catheter via which she was 
previously receiving TPN was removed by the interventional 
radiology service. On discharge she was tolerating TF well, off 
TPN, and also tolerating a stage V diet. She will continue to 
take an oral PPI, and follow up with Dr. ___ on ___.
 
Discharge Disposition:
Home With Service
 
Facility:
___
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Nausea with vomiting.
2. Malnutrition.

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital to undergo a laparascopic 
gastrostomy, which occured on ___.  You have been 
weaned from your TPN with subsequent removal of your central 
line and are now tolerating goal, nocturnal tube feedings.  You 
are now preparing for home with the following instructions:
-Some discomfort around the tube site is normal for the first 
few days after surgery.  If you experience severe, worsening 
pain, fever > 101.5°, nausea or vomiting, call your physician. 
-Dressing: The area around the tube may be washed with mild soap 
and water.  Antibiotic ointment and a dry dressing may be 
reapplied until the incision closes. When there is no drainage 
around the tube, the dressing may be omitted.
Prior to Feeding:
-The tube should be aspirated with a 60ml syringe prior to 
feeding to check for residual food.
-If more that 50 ml is aspirated, stop the feeding and notify 
the physician who has ordered your formula.

Methods of Feeding:
-Bolus: Feedings are accomplished using a 60cc syringe (without 
the plunger), allowing gravity to deliver the liquid food into 
the tube.
-Continuous Feeding: The liquid feeding is poured into a bag and 
infused into the stomach over a 24 hour period using a pump.  
You will be going home with cycled, continuous feedings over a 
12 hour period.

 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ woman status post gastric bypass, now with
G-tube placement.  Please confirm G-tube placement.

FINDINGS:  Three views of the abdomen are provided.  There is a G-tube seen
coursing into the stomach.  Contrast is seen being injected into the G-tube
and filling the gastric fundus.

IMPRESSION:  G-tube in the stomach. Contrast seen in the fundus of the
stomach.

RIGHT IJV TUNNELED CATHETER REMOVAL.  

OPERATORS:  ___, Dr. ___ and Dr. ___
(attending physician, present and supervising throughout).  

PROCEDURE:  Under aseptic conditions, local anesthesia (lidocaine 1%, 10ml)
was administered. Blunt dissection was performed around the catheter within
the tunnel. Due to the high position of the catheter's cuff within the tunnel,
a 6 mm width incision was placed about 4 cm from the catheter exit site on the
skin.  Further tissue dissection was performed via the incision site enabling
us to remove the catheter.  Pressure was placed over the right IJV at the
catheter entrance site for about seven minutes.  A 2.0 Vicryl subcuticular
suture was placed at the incision site.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated removal of right IJV tunneled catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You were admitted overnight due to ongoing nausea and trouble keeping food down after your gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been so nauseous. I can’t eat more than a few bites. I’ve been relying on the TPN through my central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your history shows you had ulcers after the bypass, which are now healed, but the nausea and poor intake have continued. We’re concerned about malnutrition, which is why you’ve needed TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve lost a lot of weight. I just can’t tolerate eating. Is there anything we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The plan is to place a gastrostomy tube—what we call a G-tube—through your abdomen into your stomach. This will let us give you nutrition directly into your stomach instead of through your veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So, like a feeding tube? Will I still be able to eat by mouth at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s a feeding tube. We’ll start with tube feeds at night. Over time, you may still be able to eat small amounts by mouth, but the tube will make sure you get enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And this is done with surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a laparoscopic procedure—small incisions, camera-guided. It’s low risk, and we do it often for patients in your situation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today. The OR schedule has you set for around noon. We’ll go over consent and prep you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee again. You just came back from surgery. The G-tube was placed successfully—no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I didn’t feel anything—must’ve been out cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, general anesthesia. The tube is in the right spot. We’ll wait until tomorrow to start feeds, after we confirm placement with a contrast study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will it hurt when I start using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some soreness around the site, like after any small surgery. But it shouldn’t be severe. We’ll manage pain with medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. I’m reviewing your imaging from last night. The gastrograffin study shows the G-tube is in the correct position in your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Does that mean we can start the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nutrition team is starting you on Fibersource HN through the tube at a low rate. We’ll increase it gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my TPN? Will I still need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already stopped the TPN. The goal is to get you fully off it. The tube feeds will replace it over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I never liked the central line. It felt like a constant reminder I wasn’t healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Once we confirm you’re doing well on tube feeds, we’ll remove the central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea or discomfort from the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, no. I don’t feel worse. Maybe a little full, but not sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’re keeping the rate low today, but tomorrow we’ll increase it. The goal is 80 cc per hour for 12 hours overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Overnight only? So I’m not hooked up all day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just overnight. That’s called cycled feeding. Gives your stomach a break during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re up to 80 cc/hr and tolerated it well last night. No issues with nausea or bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, actually slept better. I didn’t wake up hungry or sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s exactly what we want. We’re also going to remove your central line today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. Is it safe to remove it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re stable, well-nourished from the feeds, and no longer need TPN. The interventional radiology team will remove it this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your central line has been successfully removed. The site is clean, no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel it. I’m so glad it’s gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the area covered for a day or two. You’re doing really well on the G-tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try eating a little by mouth again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started you on a stage V diet—full liquids. Things like broth, yogurt, protein shakes. We’ll see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some apple juice earlier. No nausea. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. You’re off TPN, on full tube feeds, and tolerating oral intake. We’re looking at discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day—we’re getting ready to send you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel ready, but I’m a little nervous about managing the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. A nurse will come to your home to help with the overnight feeds. And you’ll have detailed instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like how to check the tube before feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll use a syringe to check for residual—any leftover formula in the stomach. If it’s more than 50 ml, you’ll pause and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dressing around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wash with mild soap and water. Apply antibiotic ointment and a dry dressing until it stops draining. Once healed, you can leave it uncovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking the pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once daily. It helps prevent ulcers and protects your stomach, especially with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. Patel in two weeks. We’ll check your weight, the tube site, and how you’re doing overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel like I’m finally on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are. You’ve made excellent progress—off TPN, on full feeds, and tolerating food. We’re proud of how far you’ve come.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just glad I can start healing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll do great. Call us if you have fever over 101.5, severe pain, or vomiting. Otherwise, rest and let the feeds do their job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge orders are in. Home health nurse will start tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send the feeding pump and supplies with you. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe this chapter is over. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Vital signs are stable—temperature normal, heart rate down from admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Abdomen is soft, no tenderness. G-tube site looks clean. You’re medically ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Just need the paperwork and I’ll head out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s being printed now. Safe journey home.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for persistent nausea and poor oral intake following gastric bypass surgery, leading to malnutrition and dependence on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). She underwent a laparoscopic gastrostomy tube placement to establish enteral feeding access. Postoperatively, she tolerated tube feeds well, reached goal nocturnal feeding rates, and was weaned off TPN. Her central line was removed, and she began tolerating a stage V diet. She was discharged home with home nursing support for tube feeds, instructions for G-tube care, and a follow-up plan with her surgeon.
